rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar doubles the bāʾ in lubadan; the other readers pronounce it light.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر بتشديد الباء، وقرأ الباقون بتخفيفها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and al-Kisāʾī read the phrases as verbs with accusative raqabah; the others read nouns, with rafʿ on fakk and iṭʿām and genitive raqabah.
rows.anchor: فك بفتح الكاف رقبة بالنصب أو أطعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two Medinan readers and Ibn ʿĀmir read fa-lā; their regional codices have fāʾ, while the other readers and their codices have wāw.
rows.anchor: فلا بالفاء، وكذا هي في مصاحف المدينة وأهل الشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most transmitters of Qunbul, including Ibn Mujāhid and Ibn Shanabūdh, report the short hamza without alif; al-Zaynabī alone reports Qunbul with lengthening.
rows.anchor: واختلف عن قنبل في أن رآه استغنى، فروى ابن مجاهد وابن شنبوذ، وأكثر الرواة عنه رأه بقصر الهمزة

rows.speaker: ابن مجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Mujāhid judged Qunbul mistaken in the long form and may therefore have declined to transmit it; al-Khuzāʿī was said to have reported it from Qunbul's companions.
rows.anchor: إلا أن ابن مجاهد غلط قنبلا في ذلك، فربما لم يأخذ به، وزعم أن الخزاعي رواه

rows.speaker: الناس
rows.claim: Critics of Ibn Mujāhid argued that an established transmission must be followed despite weak Arabic support, and that al-Khuzāʿī's book does not mention this reading.
rows.anchor: ورد الناس على ابن مجاهد في ذلك بأن الرواية إذا ثبتت وجب الأخذ بها وإن كانت حجتها في العربية ضعيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuttal is not binding: a transmitter who suspects an error need not report it except to clarify it, and a narrator's mistake does not make the underlying reading weak.
rows.anchor: ليس ما رد به على ابن مجاهد في هذا لازما فإن الراوي إذا ظن غلط المروي عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some allow three stopping lengths on the eased final hamza, analogizing it to jāʾa and shāʾa; the author rejects this because it changes the wording and corrupts the meaning.
rows.anchor: وهذا وجه لا يصح ولا يجوز لاختلاف لفظه وفساد المعنى به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Mujāhid's description of a long sound after rāʾ was misunderstood: he meant the accepted facilitation of hamza, using madd as readers commonly do to describe it.
rows.anchor: فعبر بالمدة عن التسهيل كما هي عادة القراء في إطلاق عباراتهم

rows.speaker: أبو العلاء الداني
rows.claim: Al-Dānī describes Hamza's stop as imālah on rāʾ followed by a prolonged imālah sound; the full analysis treats four successive letters as imālah and supports the correct oral reading.
rows.anchor: قال الحافظ أبو العلاء الداني في " جامع البيان ": فوقف حمزة (تراء) بإمالة فتحة الراء

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī says that interpreting Ibn Mujāhid as deleting the root's middle and final letters is unsound; turning hamza into yāʾ to say tarāyā is also reported as weak.
rows.anchor: قال الأستاذ أبو علي الفارسي في كتاب الحجة في قول ابن مجاهد: هذا إن كان يريد بالمد ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed explanation is that imālah brings rāʾ's fatḥah near kasrah, so the hamza receives the treatment of a kasrah-context hamza.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل في توجيهه: إنه لما قرب فتحة الراء من الكسرة بالإمالة أعطاها حكم المكسور

rows.speaker: طاهر بن سوار والهذلي
rows.claim: One transmitted facilitation of aʾimmah uses a single hamza followed by a slight yāʾ-like sound; many authorities describe it as a yāʾ with a partly realized kasrah.
rows.anchor: أئمة بنبرة واحدة وبعدها إشمام الياء، وعلى هذا الوجه نص طاهر بن سوار

rows.speaker: ابن شريح
rows.claim: Another group, including Ibn Shurayḥ, reads a full yāʾ after the hamza; the author notes that grammarians also treated this as their position.
rows.anchor: إلى أنها تجعل ياء خالصة، نص على ذلك أبو عبد الله بن شريح

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinnī calls al-Kisāʾī's fully realized hamza in aʾimmah an anomalous hamza reading, arguing that two hamzas do not normally meet inside one word unless both are root consonants.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن جني في باب شواذ الهمز من كتاب الخصائص له: ومن شاذ الهمز عندنا قراءة الكسائي

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī says full realization is not the proper analogy, since no one reports it in Ādam and similar words; he applies the same reasoning to aʾimmah.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر أبو علي الفارسي التحقيق قال: وليس بالوجه؛ لأنا لا نعلم أحدا ذكر التحقيق في آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The underlying form is aʾayimah, the plural of imām on the afʿilah pattern; the mīm's vowel moved to the preceding quiescent hamza, which explains why grammarians favor replacing it with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: أصلها أأيمة على وزن أفعلة جمع إمام، فنقل حركة الميم إلى الهمزة الساكنة قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command istaʿidh asks for refuge; saying aʿūdhu performs that refuge, whereas astaʿīdhu only says that one is seeking to take refuge.
rows.anchor: فمعنى استعذت بالله أطلب منه أن يعيذك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The formula astaghfiru Allāh appropriately remains a request, because forgiveness can only be granted by God, unlike refuge which the speaker takes by turning to Him.
rows.anchor: أنه يطلب المغفرة التي لا تتأتى إلا منه بخلاف العياذ

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās says Gabriel first told Muhammad to seek refuge; he replied with a formula seeking refuge in the All-Hearing, All-Knowing, then came the basmalah and the command to read.
rows.anchor: عبد الله بن عباس قال: أول ما نزل جبريل

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr calls the Ibn ʿAbbās report unusual and says its chain is weak and disconnected, so it cannot serve as proof.
rows.anchor: أبو الفداء إسماعيل بن كثير - رحمه الله - بعد إيراده: وهذا إسناد غريب

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني
rows.claim: Al-Dānī gives what the author calls the correct version from Abū Rūq through al-Ḍaḥḥāk to Ibn ʿAbbās, saying Gabriel first taught the Prophet; the excerpt ends before the account is completed.
rows.anchor: فإن الحافظ أبا عمرو الداني - رحمه الله تعالى - رواه على الصواب من حديث أبي روق

rows.speaker: أئمة أهل العراق
rows.claim: Iraqi imams who accepted the ten and eleven readings as firmly established as the seven compiled them and recited them in and out of prayer; the author says scholars agreed and none objected.
rows.anchor: كان أئمة أهل العراق الذين ثبتت عندهم قراءات العشرة والأحد عشر كثبوت هذه السبعة

rows.speaker: القاضي عياض
rows.claim: The condemnation reported by Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ against Ibn Shanabūdh concerned anomalous readings outside the Uthmanic codex, not the canonical ten.
rows.anchor: وأما الذي ذكره القاضي عياض ومن نقل كلامه من الإنكار على ابن شنبوذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reader may recite a transmitted reading he knows but must not use one he has not learned; he should neither reject nor oppose another reader for a reading known to that person.
rows.anchor: فليس له أن يقرأ بما لا يعلمه، فإن القراءة كما قال زيد بن ثابت سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven readings attributed to Nāfiʿ and ʿĀṣim are not the seven revealed aḥruf, nor do the seven readings together constitute one of those aḥruf; the author says scholars agree.
rows.anchor: فتبين بما ذكرناه أن القراءات المنسوبة إلى نافع وعاصم ليست هي الأحرف السبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings established from al-Aʿmash, Yaʿqūb, Khalaf, Abū Jaʿfar, and Shaybah stand like those of the seven for readers who establish their transmission; the author says the imams did not dispute this.
rows.anchor: بل القراءات الثابتة عن الأئمة القراء: كالأعمش ويعقوب وخلف وأبي جعفر، وشيبة

rows.speaker: المتأخرون
rows.claim: The later scholars' dispute was whether the Uthmanic codex, including the seven, ten, and other readings it contains, represents one of the seven revealed aḥruf.
rows.anchor: وإنما تنازع الناس من الخلف في المصحف العثماني الإمام الذي أجمع عليه أصحاب رسول الله

rows.speaker: صاحب التيسير وصاحب الكافي
rows.claim: The Taysīr regards both forms as sound, while al-Kāfī prefers the dammah.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب " التيسير ": وهما صحيحان. وقال في " الكافي ": الضم أحسن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers dammah as the regular and sounder form: Hamza uses it in similar hāʾs because the preceding yāʾ derives from an alif, so dammah here is more original.
rows.anchor: والضم هو القياس، وهو الأصح، فقد رواه منصوصا محمد بن يزيد الرفاعي صاحب سليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where codices seemed to add a yāʾ in bāyidin and bāyīkum, the author says the alif is extra; the following yāʾ represents hamza in connected spelling, with an initial hamza treated as medial.
rows.anchor: والصواب عندي - والله أعلم - أن الألف هي الزائدة كما زيدت في مائة ومائتين

rows.speaker: السخاوي
rows.claim: Al-Sakhāwī saw Iraqi and Syrian codices spell bāyiyah and bāyātinā with two yāʾs after the alif; he explained this as imālah written with yāʾ and omission of an alif.
rows.anchor: وقال السخاوي: وقد رأيته في المصاحف العراقية (بايية، وباييتنا) بياءين بعد الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author questions al-Sakhāwī's wording: the singular bāyāh has no alif after its yāʾ, so he likely meant the alif after hamza in the singular and after yāʾ in the plural, or a copying omission.
rows.anchor: وقوله: حذفت الألف التي بعد الياء الثانية من (بآية) فيه نظر ; لأنه ليس بعد الياء في (بآية)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most departures from standard hamza spelling follow familiar analogy or a purposeful meaning; one should assume a sound rationale and respect the early authorities.
rows.anchor: أكثره على قياس مشهور، وغالبه لمعنى مقصود، وإن لم يرد ظاهره فلا بد له من وجه مستقيم

rows.speaker: بعض الناس
rows.claim: Some explained unusual codex spellings by attributing to ʿUthmān the saying that Arabs would correct errors in the codices with their tongues.
rows.anchor: كان بعض الناس يقول في بعض ما خرج عما عرفه من القياس: هو عندنا مما قال فيه عثمان

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني
rows.claim: Al-Dānī rejects attributing that view to ʿUthmān: he would not leave a baseless writing error for Arabs to repair, since that would make writing pointless and burdensome.
rows.anchor: قال الحافظ أبو عمرو الداني: ولا يجوز عندنا أن يرى عثمان - رضي الله عنه - شيئا في المصحف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two Medinan readers and Ibn ʿĀmir pronounce the hāʾ of Allāh with ḍamma in both positions; Ruways agrees only when beginning, while the others use kasrah in both.
rows.anchor: فقرأ المدنيان، وابن عامر برفع الهاء في الحالين، وافقهم رويس في الابتداء خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read khāliqu with an alif and nominative qāf, making the following nouns genitive; the others read the verb khalaqa with accusatives.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة والكسائي وخلف، (خالق) فيها بألف وكسر اللام ورفع القاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza reads the yāʾ in bi-maṣrikhī with kasrah, a valid Banū Yarbuʿ dialect: the first yāʾ acts like a consonant after assimilation, allowing the second to take kasrah to resolve two sukūns; the author rejects those who weaken it.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة بكسر الياء، وهي لغة بني يربوع، نص على ذلك قطرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr use fatḥah on yāʾ throughout; Ruways varies by route, with al-Tammār generally matching them here, in Hajj, and Zumar, while the Abū al-Ṭayyib route differs; others use ḍammah.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو بفتح الياء في الأربعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī read both verbs in the jussive; the other readers read them in the indicative.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أبو عمرو والكسائي بجزمهما، وقرأ الباقون برفعهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī use kasrah at the start of all four words; Ḥafṣ agrees except on bukiyyan, while the other readers use ḍammah.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة والكسائي بكسر، أوائل الأربعة، وافقهما حفص إلا في وبكيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read khalaqnāka with plural nūn and alif; the others read khalaqtuka with singular wording.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة والكسائي، (خلقناك) بالنون والألف على لفظ الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb, and Warsh read liyahaba with yāʾ after the lām. Qālūn varies by route, though many sources transmit the yāʾ form.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أبو عمرو ويعقوب وورش، بالياء بعد اللام، واختلف عن قالون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author corrects claims limiting the yāʾ form to one of Yaʿqūb's two narrators: it belongs to Yaʿqūb in full, except al-Walīd's hamza reading.
rows.anchor: بل الصواب أن الياء فيه ليعقوب بكماله. نعم الوليد عن يعقوب بالهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With a fatḥah hamza preceded by ḍammah at a verb's start, Abū Jaʿfar and Warsh generally replace it with wāw.
rows.anchor: فاتفق أبو جعفر وورش على إبدالها واوا نحو

rows.speaker: ابن وردان
rows.claim: Ibn Wardān differs on yuʾayyid bi-naṣrihi: some routes preserve hamza, apparently to avoid three weak letters in succession after the doubled yāʾ, while most substitute wāw in line with the rule.
rows.anchor: واختلف ابن وردان في حرف واحد من ذلك، وهو (يؤيد بنصره) في آل عمران، فروى ابن شبيب

rows.speaker: ورش
rows.claim: For muʾadhdhin, al-Aṣbahānī preserves Warsh's hamza, apparently because of its link with fa-adhdhin; al-Azraq instead substitutes according to the usual rule.
rows.anchor: واختلف أيضا عن ورش في حرف واحد، وهو (مؤذن) في الأعراف ويوسف. فروى عنه الأصبهاني

rows.speaker: حفص
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ uniquely replaces a final root hamza in huzuwan at ten occurrences and also in kufuwan.
rows.anchor: فإن حفصا اختص بإبدالها في (هزوا) ، وهو في عشرة مواضع

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar commonly changes an open hamza preceded by kasrah to yāʾ, including khāṭiʾah; some routes of Ibn Wardān and Zayd preserve hamza in khāṭiʾah, al-khāṭiʾah, miʾah, and fiʾah.
rows.anchor: وكذلك (يبدلها) في (خاطئة، والخاطئة، ومئة، وفئة) وتثنيتهما، وانفرد الشطوي عن ابن هارون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar's reading of mawṭiyan varies among transmitters: some report substitution and some hamza; the author accepts both, has read both, and adopts both.
rows.anchor: والوجهان صحيحان، بهما قرأت، وبهما آخذ، والله أعلم.

rows.speaker: أهل الأداء
rows.claim: Teachers forbid stopping between a genitive annexation and its governing noun; they rejected the defense that such a written break merely marked a hypothetical pause.
rows.anchor: إنما ذلك لو وقع الوقف لكان هذا. وأما أن يجوز قطع المضاف من المضاف إليه فلا

rows.speaker: أهل الأداء
rows.claim: The sixth rule requires a reader to finish the second reciter's reading to the end of the verse before restoring anything omitted from the first, avoiding an unmarked splice of two readers.
rows.anchor: وأما إتمام الخلف إلى آخره فلا يجوز عندهم إذا قرأ القارئ ثم قرأ بعده القارئ الآخر

rows.speaker: القيجاطي
rows.claim: The seventh rule's preferred order is Warsh before Qālūn and Qunbul before al-Bazzī; teachers tolerate other orders, though following the authors' order is best.
rows.anchor: وهو أن يبدأ بورش قبل قالون وبقنبل قبل البزي بحسب ترتيبهم فهذا أسهل الأوجه السبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the proposed rules remain insufficient: stopping at “woe to those who pray” or beginning a fragment about believing in God can mislead; he also reports a teacher rebuking someone who stopped after “the hands of Abū Lahab” merely to display madd lengths.
rows.anchor: وكذلك في الاقتصار على الستة الباقية إذ ليست وافية بالقصد تجنب ما لا يليق مما يوهم غير المعنى المراد

rows.speaker: محمد بن بضحان
rows.claim: The teacher Muḥammad ibn Baḍḥān rebuked a man who stopped after “the hands of Abū Lahab” and repeated it to demonstrate all the madd lengths.
rows.anchor: وبلغني عن شيخ شيوخنا الأستاذ بدر الدين محمد بن بضحان رحمه الله وكان كثير التدبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Four conditions are essential for combining readings: observe stopping and starting, perform well, and avoid تركيب (mixing readings into an invalid composite).
rows.anchor: أن الذي يشترط على جامعي القراءات أربعة شروط لا بد منها، وهي رعاية الوقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fixed reader order is unnecessary; the skilled reader may begin with any reader but should resume that same reader after a pause, which better avoids mixing and shows command.
rows.anchor: لا يلتزم تقديم شخص بعينه ولكن من إذا وقف على وجه لقارئ ابتدأ لذلك القارئ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some combine readings in graduated order: move from shorter to longer madd, or from longer to shorter, and likewise sequence degrees of imālah and hamza treatment.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم كان يراعي في الجمع نوعا آخر، وهو التناسب فكان إذا ابتدأ مثلا بالقصر أتى بالمرتبة التي فوقه
